title: Remembering God in the Promised Land

date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Deut 7:1 lists seven nations — Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites — “greater and mightier than thou.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:1, read in full.

claims.claim: The seven-name list differs from the six-name lists elsewhere (Deut 20:17; Ex 3:8, 17; 23:23; 33:2), which omit the Girgashites; ten nations are named in Gen 15:19–21.
claims.evidence: K&D on Deut 7:1 (seven here, as in Josh 3:10; 24:11; six elsewhere); Cogan fn 22 (three in Ex 23:28; five in Ex 13:5; ten in Gen 15:19–21), read in part.

claims.claim: Deut 7:2 commands smiting, utter destruction, no covenant, and no mercy toward the seven nations when the LORD delivers them.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:2, read in full; BDB H2763 *ḥāram* (Deut 7:2 listed twice in the verse).

claims.claim: *Ḥāram* (H2763), Hiphil, means “ban, devote, exterminate”; in Deut 7:2 the infinitive absolute + imperfect (*haḥărēm taḥărîmēm*) intensifies the command.
claims.evidence: BDB H2763, read in full (BibleHub lexicon page).

claims.claim: The stated reason for the ban is religious: intermarriage will turn Israel’s sons away to serve other gods (7:3–4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:3–4, read in full; K&D on Deut 7:1 (“for he will cause thy son to turn away from behind me”).

claims.claim: Deut 7:5 commands destroying their altars, breaking down images, cutting down groves (Asherim), and burning graven images with fire.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:5, read in full; K&D on Deut 7:5 (cf. Ex 34:13; 23:24).

claims.claim: Israel’s election (7:6–8) rests on the LORD’s love and the oath to the fathers, not on numbers (“ye were the fewest of all people”) or merit.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:6–8, read in full; K&D on Deut 7:6; JFB on Deut 7:6–10.

claims.claim: Deut 7:9–10 states that the LORD is “the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy… to a thousand generations,” and repays haters “to his face… he will not be slack.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:9–10, read in full; K&D on Deut 7:9 (developing Ex 20:5–6).

claims.claim: Deut 7:12–16 promises blessings for hearkening: fruit of womb and land, corn, wine, oil, cattle, no barrenness, and removal of sickness.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:12–16, read in full; K&D on Deut 7:12 (cf. Ex 23:25–27).

claims.claim: The “evil diseases of Egypt” (7:15) are identified by K&D as chiefly the malignant leprosy called elephantiasis, possibly plague and other malignant diseases.
claims.evidence: K&D on Deut 7:15 (cf. Deut 28:27; Hengstenberg; Pruner). A commentary identification, not a textual statement.

claims.claim: Deut 7:16 commands consuming all the peoples the LORD delivers, with no pity, and warns that serving their gods “will be a snare unto thee.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:16, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 7:17–24 answers fear of the nations’ size by remembering Egypt, promises the hornet (7:20), and gradual dispossession “by little and little” (7:22), with kings delivered and their names destroyed (7:24).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:17–24, read in full; K&D on Deut 7:17–26 (cf. Ex 23:27–30).

claims.claim: Deut 7:22’s gradualism (“by little and little”) sits in tension with the total-destruction command of 7:2 and with the intermarriage ban of 7:3, which presupposes survivors.
claims.evidence: Lilley, pp. 174–175 (v. 22 implies gradual extension; Mayes finds vv. 2 and 3 inconsistent), read in full; Peters (the intermarriage ban presupposes survivors), read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 7:25–26 forbids desiring or taking the silver and gold on graven images, “lest thou be a cursed thing like it” — the taker falls under the ban.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:25–26, read in full; K&D on Deut 7:25–26 (cf. Josh 7, Achan).

claims.claim: The text gives the reason for the ban as the danger of idolatry (7:4), not as an ethnic rationale.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:4, read in full; cf. Deut 20:18. See the shared record §4.1.

claims.claim: Deut 8:1–2 states the forty years were “to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 8:1–2, read in full; JFB on Deut 8:2–3.

claims.claim: Deut 8:3 states that manna taught that “man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 8:3, read in full; JFB on Deut 8:2–3.

claims.claim: Deut 8:4 states that raiment “waxed not old” and the foot did not swell “these forty years.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 8:4, read in full; JFB on Deut 8:4 (a miraculous preservation).

claims.claim: Deut 8:5 compares the LORD’s chastening to a father chastening his son.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 8:5, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 8:7–9 describes the good land: brooks, fountains, wheat, barley, vines, fig trees, pomegranates, oil olive, honey, iron, and brass (copper ore).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 8:7–9, read in full; JFB on Deut 8:7–9 (“brass — not the alloy brass, but the ore of copper”).

claims.claim: Deut 8:11–18 warns that prosperity — fullness, houses, herds, silver, gold — lifts up the heart to forget the LORD, and that wealth is God’s gift “that he may establish his covenant.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 8:11–18, read in full; JFB on Deut 8:11–20.

claims.claim: Deut 8:19–20 warns that forgetting the LORD and following other gods brings perishing “as the nations which the LORD destroyeth before your face.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 8:19–20, read in full.

claims.claim: Deut 9:1–3 states Israel will cross the Jordan against the Anakim and cities “fenced up to heaven,” with the LORD going before “as a consuming fire.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 9:1–3, read in full; JFB on Deut 9:1 (“this day” means “this time”).

claims.claim: Deut 9:4–6 states the land is given not for Israel’s righteousness but for the nations’ wickedness and the oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; “thou art a stiffnecked people.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 9:4–6, read in full; JFB on Deut 9:4–6.

claims.claim: Deut 9:7–21 retells Horeb, the forty days without bread or water, the tables “written with the finger of God,” the molten calf, the breaking of the tables, the second forty days, Aaron’s peril, and the calf ground to dust into the brook.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 9:7–21, read in full; JFB on Deut 9:12–29.

claims.claim: Deut 9:25’s forty days describe the second intercession of 9:18 in fuller detail, not a third fast.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 9:25 (comparison with Num 14:5). A commentary reading, not a textual certainty.

claims.claim: Deut 9:21’s brook “that descended out of the mount” is read by JFB as the water of the smitten rock (Ex 17:5–6), possibly flowing miles from the rock through the wadies.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 9:21 (citing Wilson, *Land of the Bible*; cf. Ps 78:15–16; 1 Cor 10:4). A commentary reading.

claims.claim: Deut 9:22 names Taberah, Massah, and Kibroth-hattaavah as places where Israel provoked the LORD to wrath.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 9:22, read in full; JFB on Deut 9:22 (cross-references Num 11; Ex 17:7).

claims.claim: Deut 9:23 states that at Kadesh-barnea Israel rebelled, “believed him not, nor hearkened to his voice.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 9:23, read in full; JFB on Deut 9:22–23.

claims.claim: Deut 9:26–29 records Moses’ intercession appealing to redemption (“thy people and thine inheritance”), to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to what Egypt would say.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 9:26–29, read in full; JFB on Deut 9:25–29.

claims.claim: Deut 10:1–5 states that Moses hewed two tables “like unto the first,” made an ark of shittim wood, and put the tables in the ark — “and there they be, as the LORD commanded me.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 10:1–5, read in full; JFB on Deut 10:1–5.

claims.claim: The ark’s timing differs between Deut 10:3 (made before the ascent) and Ex 37:1 (made by Bezaleel after the return); JFB resolves it by Moses instructing Bezaleel beforehand.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 10:3. A commentary resolution of a genuine sequence difference, recorded as Probable.

claims.claim: Deut 10:4 states God wrote on the second tables “according to the first writing, the ten commandments,” and 10:10 states Moses stayed forty days and the LORD “would not destroy thee.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 10:4, 10, read in full; JFB on Deut 10:4–5 (“not Moses… but God Himself”).

claims.claim: Deut 10:6–7 lists the stations Beeroth of the children of Jaakan, Mosera (Aaron’s death and burial; Eleazar succeeds), Gudgodah, and Jotbath, in a different order from Num 33:31–33.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 10:6–7, read in full; JFB on Deut 10:6–9 (same stations, different order).

claims.claim: JFB’s explanation of the order difference is that Numbers lists the first visit during the southward wandering and Deuteronomy the second passage to compass Edom.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 10:6–9 (citing Robinson). A commentary explanation, not a textual statement.

claims.claim: Deut 10:8–9 states the LORD separated Levi to bear the ark, stand, minister, and bless, with no part or inheritance, “the LORD is his inheritance.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 10:8–9, read in full; JFB on Deut 10:6–9.

claims.claim: Deut 10:12–15 states the requirement — fear, walk, love, serve, keep “for thy good” — and grounds it in the God who owns “the heaven and the heaven of heavens” yet chose the fathers.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 10:12–15, read in full; JFB on Deut 10:10–22.

claims.claim: Deut 10:16 commands “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked,” teaching the spiritual meaning of the rite.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 10:16, read in full; JFB on Deut 10:16 (citing Rom 2:25, 29; 1 Pet 3:21). The text is Established; the spiritual reading is Probable as a commentary judgment.

claims.claim: Deut 10:17–19 states the LORD is “God of gods, and Lord of lords,” impartial, executing judgment for the fatherless and widow, loving the stranger — and commands Israel to love the stranger because “ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 10:17–19, read in full; JFB on Deut 10:16–22.

claims.claim: Deut 10:22 states the fathers went down into Egypt “with threescore and ten persons” and the LORD “hath made thee as the stars of heaven for multitude.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 10:22, read in full; JFB on Deut 10:22.

claims.claim: Deut 11:1–9 grounds the exhortation in eyewitness experience: “I speak not with your children which have not known… But your eyes have seen all the great acts of the LORD.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 11:1–9 (text as quoted in full in JFB on Deut 11); JFB on Deut 11:2–9.

claims.claim: Deut 11:4 and 11:6 recall the Red Sea overthrow and Dathan and Abiram swallowed by the earth with households, tents, and substance.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 11:4, 6 (text as quoted in full in JFB on Deut 11).

claims.claim: Deut 11:10–12 contrasts Egypt (watered by foot, “as a garden of herbs”) with Canaan (hills and valleys, “drinketh water of the rain of heaven,” a land the LORD cares for always).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 11:10–12 (text as quoted in full in JFB on Deut 11); JFB on Deut 11:10–12 (the foot-operated sluice).

claims.claim: Deut 11:13–17 makes the first and latter rain conditional on loving and serving the LORD, and threatens a shut heaven, no fruit, and perishing quickly for apostasy.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 11:13–17 (text as quoted in full in JFB on Deut 11); JFB on Deut 11:14 (early rain Sept–Oct, latter rain Mar–Apr).

claims.claim: Deut 11:18–21 commands laying up the words in heart and soul, binding them as signs, teaching children at all times, and writing them on doorposts and gates.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 11:18–21 (text as quoted in full in JFB on Deut 11); JFB on Deut 11:18–25 (cf. Deut 6).

claims.claim: Deut 11:22–25 promises the boundary — wilderness, Lebanon, Euphrates, uttermost sea — and that “no man shall be able to stand before you.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 11:22–25 (text as quoted in full in JFB on Deut 11); JFB on Deut 11:24 (Lebanon the northern limit; Euphrates the east; the Mediterranean the uttermost sea).

claims.claim: Deut 11:26–32 sets “a blessing and a curse” before Israel, to be pronounced on Gerizim (blessing) and Ebal (curse), “over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh.”
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 11:26–32 (text as quoted in full in JFB on Deut 11); JFB on Deut 11:26–32 (cf. Deut 27:11).

claims.claim: Deut 11:29 names Gerizim for blessing and Ebal for curse, the same pair as Deut 27:12–13; the 27:4 Ebal/Gerizim textual variant belongs to Category 7.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 11:29 (text as quoted in JFB on Deut 11); Deut 27:12–13 (cross-reference). The variant is recorded in the Phase 2 Correction Record and Category 7’s shared record, not decided here.

claims.claim: The herem command of Deut 7:2 is a lethal command as written (smite + utterly destroy + no covenant + no mercy); it must not be neutralised by asserting hyperbole.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:2, read in full; BDB H2763, read in full; Lilley, read in full; shared record §§0–1.

claims.claim: Deut 7:2–3 and 7:22 together show the text presupposing Canaanites still present after the commanded destruction (intermarriage ban; gradual dispossession).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 7:2–3, 22, read in full; Lilley, pp. 174–175; Peters, read in full. A textual observation; the inference from it is clm-deu-03-051.

claims.claim: Scholars disagree whether the tension in clm-deu-03-050 shows rhetorical heightening (Peters, Moberly, Earl) or a staged/gradual conquest, and neither reading settles historicity by itself.
claims.evidence: Peters, read in full; Lilley (Mayes), read in full; shared record §2.

claims.claim: Surveys record a sharp Iron I increase in hill-country sites (roughly 30 in the Late Bronze Age to roughly 250 in Iron Age I), with small unwalled villages, four-room houses, collared-rim jars, and scarce pig bones.
claims.evidence: Rendsburg, “The Emergence of Israel in the Land of Canaan” (read in full, re-grounding session 2026-11-20 — Rutgers PDF, *Ancient Israel* ch. 3, pp. 59–91: ~30 Late Bronze settlements → ~250 Iron Age I; “This expansion cannot be due to natural population growth, but must rather indicate the arrival of a new people”; four-room houses; collared-rim jars; near-total absence of pig bones at early Israelite sites; unwalled settlements). Bloch-Smith & Nakhai (1999) — search excerpt only (the 45,000 population figure is theirs, not Rendsburg’s — it is NOT in this claim). Capped Probable: survey data via a scholarly synthesis, not the primary surveys.

claims.claim: Whether the Iron I settlement pattern reflects conquest, peaceful settlement, or indigenous ethnogenesis is debated; no single rapid conquest matching the narrated herem is archaeologically established.
claims.evidence: Rendsburg, “The Emergence of Israel in the Land of Canaan” (read in full, re-grounding session 2026-11-20): conquest model “Hardly anyone today... would countenance this view” (contradicted by evidence); “peaceful infiltration/settlement” (Alt) “is the one which has stood the test of time”; Mendenhall/Gottwald peasant-revolt (autochthonous) “controverted as the sole explanation”. Finkelstein (1988, p. 348) and Finkelstein & Silberman (2001) — search excerpts only (the indigenous-ethnogenesis side as reported); shared record §3. Capped Debated as a live interpretive dispute.

claims.claim: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) names Israel as a people in Canaan (“Israel is laid waste, its seed is not”) — the terminus ante quem for Israel’s presence.
claims.evidence: source-merneptah-stele (reused verified source, Exodus dossier §6.1).

claims.claim: The Mesha Stele (mid-9th century BCE) uses the same herem root for devoting Nebo’s population (7,000) to Ashtar-Chemosh, proving the practice and vocabulary were regional, not Israelite-invented.
claims.evidence: Lilley, pp. 176–177, read in full; Cogan fn 18, read in part (Ahituv; Smelik, *COS* 2.138).

claims.claim: “Holy war” is a modern scholarly label, not a biblical term; Younger and Craigie argue it is best avoided for Israel’s wars.
claims.evidence: Lilley, pp. 171–173, read in full (citing von Rad; Smend; Younger 1990, 259; Craigie 1978, 49); Cogan fn 2, read in part (de Vaux; Younger).

claims.claim: The text frames the herem as divine judgment on wickedness (Deut 9:4–5) and warns Israel of the same fate if apostate (Deut 8:19–20); the ethical appraisal of that frame is a separate analysis from the historical and rhetorical ones.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 9:4–5; 8:19–20, read in full; shared record §4. The ethical judgment itself is not decided in this dossier.

claims.claim: JFB reads the 11:24 boundary grant as fulfilled to Solomon.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 11:24 (“Their grant of dominion extended so far, and the right was fulfilled to Solomon”). A commentary reading, not a textual statement.

connections.note: The same driving-out, no-covenant, hornet, and gradual-dispossession instructions in the Book of the Covenant.
The same prohibitions — no covenant, no intermarriage, destroy the altars — given at Sinai.
The ten-nation list of the patriarchal promise, against which the seven-name list is set.
Jericho: the herem carried out — “they utterly destroyed all that was in the city.”
*Sĕgullâ* — “a peculiar treasure… a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation.”
“A chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people.”
Visiting iniquity / mercy to thousands — K&D: Deut 7:9–10 develops Ex 20:5–6.
The hornet promise, given in the same words.
“I sent the hornet before you” — the promise recalled as fulfilled.
The *ḥērem* devotion law: what is devoted is unredeemable; a devoted person dies.
Achan took “of the accursed thing” — the 7:26 warning carried out.
The manna given: “What is this? … it is the bread which the LORD hath given you.”
Jesus quotes Deut 8:3 in the temptation: “Man shall not live by bread alone.”
The same quotation in Luke’s temptation account.
The bread-of-life discourse cites the manna tradition (“He gave them bread from heaven”).
The same statement: raiment not waxing old, shoes not waxing old, forty years.
“Whom the LORD loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth” — the father-chastening image (cf. Heb 12:5–6, which quotes Proverbs).
The same “good land” description — houses, wells, vineyards, olive trees not planted by Israel.
“Beware lest thou forget the LORD” — the same warning, in the same words.
“Ye shall soon utterly perish” — the same sanction, with heaven and earth as witness.
The spies’ report: fenced cities and the Anakim (“we were in our own sight as grasshoppers”).
The calf made: “Up, make us gods, which shall go before us.”
Moses descends, breaks the tables, burns and grinds the calf.
The forty days and forty nights in the mount.
Forty days and forty nights, “he did neither eat bread, nor drink water.”
The tables “written with the finger of God.”
Moses’ intercession for the people as the parallel to his prayer for Aaron.
Taberah: the fire of the LORD at the uttermost parts of the camp.
Massah: “Is the LORD among us, or not?”
Kibroth-hattaavah: the quails and the plague.
Kadesh-barnea: the murmuring and refusal to go up.
Moses’ intercession with the same arguments: the patriarchs, and what Egypt would say.
The second tables hewn “like unto the first,” carried up the mount.
“He wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.”
The ark of shittim wood, and the testimony put in the ark.
The same stations (Bene-jaakan, Moseroth, Hor-hagidgad, Jotbathah) in a different order.
Levi has no inheritance; “I am thy part and thine inheritance.”
“What doth the LORD require of thee” — Micah’s triad against Deuteronomy’s fivefold requirement.
“Circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit” — Paul’s use of the circumcised heart (JFB cites Rom 2:25, 29).
“Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart.”
“O give thanks unto the God of gods… the Lord of lords.”
“Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him… Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child.”
“Thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”
“Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and serve him, and shalt swear by his name” — the same formula.
“All the souls of the house of Jacob, which came into Egypt, were threescore and ten.”
The Red Sea overthrow: “the waters returned, and covered the chariots, and the horsemen.”
Dathan and Abiram: the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them.
“The LORD shall open unto thee his good treasure, the heaven to give the rain unto thy land in his season.”
“Let us now fear the LORD our God, that giveth rain, both the former and the latter, in his season.”
Solomon’s prayer: “When heaven is shut up, and there is no rain, because they have sinned against thee.”
Words in the heart, bound as signs, taught to children, written on doorposts — the same formula.
“There shall not any man be able to stand before thee all the days of thy life” — the promise repeated to Joshua.
The same boundary: wilderness, Lebanon, Euphrates, “unto the great sea.”
The same boundary promised to Abraham: “from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates.”
The tribes on Gerizim (blessing) and Ebal (curse).
“I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing.”
The ceremony carried out: the altar on Ebal, the law read to all Israel with the strangers.
Abram at “the plain of Moreh” by Shechem — the same place named in 11:30.
